newsitem.title: USA: Expert sees no police conspiracy in Simpson case.
newsitem.headline: Expert sees no police conspiracy in Simpson case.

text.p: One of America's leading forensic scientists testified via videotape on Friday at the O.J. Simpson civil trial that he found no sign police planted evidence to frame the former football star for murder.
Expert Henry Lee's testimony dealt a blow to the defence theory of a police conspiracy on the same day Simpson was due to take the witness stand for a second round of testimony.
"You have no independent knowledge that any officer in this case planted evidence, do you?" plaintiffs' attorney Edward Medvene asked.
"I have no independent knowledge, I only report scientific facts," replied Lee, chief criminalist for the state of Connecticut.
Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 in the murders of his ex-wife and her friend, is now battling a wrongful-death civil lawsuit brought by the victims' families.

With Simpson set to take the witness stand on Friday afternoon, the plaintiffs' attorneys asked Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki to bar Simpson's lawyers from asking him about allegations that Nicole Brown Simpson used drugs, drank excessively and was promiscuous.
Fujisaki denied the motion, but restricted Simpson to testifying on those subjects only so far as it helped him to prove he had no motive for the June 1994 murders.

Lee, who testified as a key defence witness in Simpson's criminal trial and was called by Simpson's attorneys in the civil case, had bolstered the defence team's evidence-planting allegations on Thursday when he testified there was "something wrong" with the police handling of blood samples in the case.
And on Friday, Lee said under cross-examination: "In the past, we have some law officers who plant evidence for no reason."

Lee's testimony, which was videotaped last year after he refused to travel to California to testify in person at the civil trial, preceded Simpson's scheduled appearance on Friday on the witness stand. Simpson was one of the last defence witnesses scheduled to testify.
With the trial nearing an end, legal analysts said Simpson's final stint on the witness stand was certain to be a major deciding factor in whether he wins or loses the case.

The defence effort to "rehabilitate" Simpson in the eyes of the jury will be followed by a critical round of cross-examination by the families' attorneys, who are expected to hammer away at inconsistencies and contradictions in his past statements.

Simpson's attorneys plan to wrap up their case on Monday, and closing arguments could begin by the end of next week. The case is expected to go to the jury before the end of January, after just three months of testimony -- a far cry from the nine months it took in Simpson's criminal trial.
If at least nine of the 12 jurors find him responsible for the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, Simpson could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages.

Simpson, who chose not to take the witness stand during his criminal trial, finished his first bruising round of testimony last Nov. 26 without a single question from his own attorneys, a move that most legal analysts thought was a tactical mistake.
But Simpson's defence team on Friday was expected to try to undo the damage by painting a more sympathetic portrait of Simpson as an innocent man wrongly accused.
Fujisaki, the no-nonsense jurist presiding over the case, has banned cameras from the courtroom, but dozens of camera crews swarmed over the lawn outside the Santa Monica courthouse.
A few demonstrators and curiosity seekers turned out, but it was a far more subdued scene than the circus-like atmosphere that surrounded the first trial.
As he arrived at the Santa Monica courthouse, Simpson smiled and waved at a handful of supporters. But one anti-Simpson protester yelled "O.J. is a murderer!"
